question: Croup most commonly affects children between 6 months and 3 years of age, characteristically produces a barking (seal-like) cough and inspiratory stridor that worsen at night, and the AP neck X-ray shows the 'steeple sign' due to subglottic narrowing.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is true. Croup (acute laryngotracheobronchitis) has a peak at 18 months (range 6 months–3 years), is caused mainly by parainfluenza virus type 1, presents with the classic barking cough and inspiratory stridor (worse at night), and produces the steeple sign on AP neck/chest X-ray from inflammatory subglottic narrowing.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. All three features are accurate: the 6-month to 3-year age peak (with 18 months most common), the barking nocturnal cough with inspiratory stridor (from parainfluenza-induced subglottic oedema), and the steeple sign on AP X-ray from narrowed subglottis. These are the canonical distinguishing features of croup.
